utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of one of the great English novels.
Over the course of this series, we're going inside Dickens's extraordinary achievement — a novel of fog, chancery, and consequence.
A novel that holds the intimate and the panoramic in one vast, breathing structure.
I'm joined today by three readers who know this book with unusual depth and love.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose life's work has been the moral imagination of the Victorian novel.
He reads Bleak House as a story about individual character tested to its limits — and he brings to it a formidable and sometimes bracingly contrarian intelligence.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels in audio than almost anyone alive.
He hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score — for rhythm, timing, and the places where the prose is written specifically to be spoken aloud.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She brings the reader's eye — the sense of what stops you, moves you, makes you re-read a sentence twice.
In this opening segment, we begin where the novel asks us to begin — with atmosphere, with setting, with the way a house and a world are established before any plot has properly moved.
What strikes me first, returning to Bleak House, is how confident Dickens is about the power of place.
He does not hurry toward event.
He builds a world first — and demands that we inhabit it.
Now, Esther's account of arriving at Bleak House for the first time is, on its surface, a cheerful domestic inventory.
Birds in frames staring at a trout, portraits of strangers distributed through the rooms, angels conveying a complacent gentleman to heaven with some difficulty.
But underneath the comedy, Dickens is doing something precise and generous.
He is establishing Bleak House as a sanctuary — a place of genuine warmth in a novel where warmth will be tested severely.
Listen to how Esther closes her first impression of the house.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House."
That phrase — a low accompaniment to everything we heard — is not decoration.
It tells us that the house itself is musical — that it resonates.
Edmund is absolutely right about the musicality, and I'd go further — that passage is written to be read aloud.
That accumulation of "with its" — three times, four times — it's an incantation.
Dickens is casting a spell over the reader, over Esther, over the house itself.
And what I love about the inventory that precedes it — the surprised birds staring at the trout, the angels hauling the complacent gentleman heavenward with some difficulty — is the comic deadpan.
Dickens cannot resist that parenthesis: "with some difficulty."
Three words that make the angels absurd and endearing simultaneously.
He's a very funny writer who is also a very serious one — and the comedy here earns the warmth of that closing sentence.
What moves me in that passage is the detail about the rose-leaves and sweet lavender stored wherever there's a drawer.
It's almost invisible — a small aside — but it tells you everything about Jarndyce as a host.
Someone has thought about what a drawer smells like when you open it.
That's care.
And yet — and this is what Bleak House does almost from its first pages — that warmth is immediately shadowed.
Because the novel gives us another house — Chesney Wold — and another woman, and a very different relationship to a building's past.
There is a passage — the crippled lady, day after day, walking the terrace at Chesney Wold.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
That is a curse.
A house and a family placed under a sentence — and the novel knows it will deliver on that sentence.
What Caroline has done there is identify something central to this novel's method — the way it holds two registers at once.
Warmth and dread.
Bleak House — even the name — promises both at once.
And the curse passage is remarkable for its repetition.
"I will walk here" — three times.
It has the structure of liturgy.
Dickens understood that when we wish to bind the future, we reach for ritual language.
And she never complains, this woman.
Dickens is quite clear — she never spoke to any one of being crippled or of being in pain.
She just walks.
Up and down, up and down — that repetition is exhausting just to read.
As a performer, I find the silence between her and her husband almost unbearable — she has, on no persuasion, opened her lips to him since that night.
And then she drops.
And instead of receiving comfort — she delivers prophecy.
Atmosphere, curse, domestic warmth — and we haven't yet touched what the novel does with human beings who have no warmth, no home, no name.
There is a boy called Jo.
His testimony at an inquest is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the whole novel.
Dickens gives us his name — Jo — and then tells us: no father, no mother, no friends.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words — and an entire life accounted for.
That is where we'll pick up next — with Jo, with poverty, with what the novel insists we see.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see how it works and why it still matters.
Today we're in the thick of it — corruption, despair, and the slow destruction of a young man by a legal system designed to consume him.
With me are three people I trust to do justice to the material.
Sir Edmund Leigh — retired Oxford don, moralist, and a reader who believes Dickens's greatness lies in character, not polemic.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has given voice to more great novels than perhaps anyone alive.
And Caroline Woodcourt — critic and passionate re-reader of classic fiction, whose attention to the verbal music of a sentence is, in my experience, unmatched.
We begin today with the passages that show Dickens at his most unflinching — poverty, legal predation, and the human cost of both.
What strikes me first, surveying these passages together, is how Dickens orchestrates moral weight without ever quite preaching.
Take the brickmaker's great speech — and it is a speech, a formal oration delivered from a floor of squalor.
Dickens does not place the indictment in the mouth of a reformer or a narrator.
He places it in the mouth of the man himself — brutal, articulate, and utterly beyond consolation.
The passage reads, in part —
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks. How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!"
The man pre-empts every question Mrs. Pardiggle might ask — he catalogues his own degradation before she can.
That is not the voice of a victim seeking sympathy — it is the voice of a man who has dispensed with illusion.
Edmund, I have read that speech — literally read it, for the audiobook — and I will tell you, it is fiendishly difficult.
The rhythm is all confrontation — every sentence dares you to respond, and every sentence answers itself before you can.
"We've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides."
When you reach that line — and you must let it land — the comedy of the speech falls away entirely.
Dickens gives the man the blackest possible humour, and then makes you feel ashamed for noticing the humour at all.
That is virtuoso writing — entertainment weaponised into moral shock.
What I cannot stop thinking about is the passage that comes just after — Esther and Ada with the dying child.
After the brickmaker's great rhetorical storm, Dickens gives us four words.
Just four.
Ada bends to touch the baby's face, and —
"As she did so, I saw what happened and drew her back. The child died."
Every time I read that sentence, I stop.
Not because it is elaborate — because it is not.
The reticence is the point — and the devastation.
Caroline is precisely right, and it connects to something about Dickens's method that I think is misunderstood.
People speak of Dickens as melodramatic — as a writer who excess is a governing principle.
But these passages show the opposite truth: his restraint, when he deploys it, is absolute.
The same precision governs his portrait of Tulkinghorn.
The man is described not as wicked but as simply — absent.
Dickens writes —
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
A shell. A case. No music audible at all.
That is more frightening than any outright villain Dickens ever drew.
The musical instrument simile is extraordinary — and I mean that in the performer's sense.
When you read Tulkinghorn aloud, you realise there is almost no register to play him in.
The absence of tone IS the tone.
He has shown, Dickens tells us, neither patience nor impatience, neither attention nor abstraction.
He has shown nothing but his shell.
Tulkinghorn and Vholes belong to the same genus — but Vholes is in some ways the more insidious creation.
Tulkinghorn at least doesn't pretend to serve his victims.
Vholes wraps his predation in the language of professional duty — and Dickens is forensic about it.
He says to Esther —
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account."
The capitalised I — Dickens means us to hear the emphasis, to hear the self-congratulation disguised as candour.
He openly declares Richard's affairs are in a very bad way — and then cheerfully greets Richard the moment he walks in.
The pivot is devastating in its comedy and its horror simultaneously.
The Vholes pivot is a genuinely Dickensian coup de théâtre — and I say that as one not naturally inclined to French terms.
But I want to turn, if I may, to Sir Leicester Dedlock — because these passages contain a moment of genuine moral rehabilitation.
Leicester has been comic, pompous, absurd throughout the novel.
And then Dickens writes this —
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
His fidelity, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own pride — these things transcend class entirely.
This is not social programme — this is moral imagination at its purest.
Edmund raises Leicester, and that's right — but let me stay a moment longer with Bucket, because that passage of his is one of the great persuasion speeches in the novel.
Bucket is performing, yes — he always performs — but the urgency is absolutely genuine.
He says to Jarndyce —
"If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to desperation."
Notice that formal "Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet" — even now, even in crisis, Bucket deploys the full title.
It's professional reflex, of course — but it also signals that he has Jarndyce's full measure.
Then the clock — one o'clock, then another hour gone, then worth a thousand pound instead of a hundred — the pressure mounts with every sentence.
Dickens could have written thrillers, and did.
And Esther is the hinge of that Bucket scene — she is what Lady Dedlock might still respond to.
A young lady that she has a tenderness for — Bucket says that without explanation, and Jarndyce cannot ask.
The whole web of secrets in the novel — the Chancery web and the family secret both — are held in that one circumspect phrase.
And the weight falls on Esther — again.
What these passages together suggest — and I don't think this is overstatement — is a novelist in complete command of register.
From the brickmaker's furious catechism to the baby's four-word death — from Vholes's parasitic punctilio to Leicester's unexpected dignity — Dickens moves without warning and without apology.
That's the novel's genius — and that's what we'll keep exploring.
Thank you to Sir Edmund, Oliver, and Caroline — and thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.
Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's great novel apart, passage by passage, and try to understand why it still holds us so completely.
Today's deep dive takes us into one of the novel's most quietly electrifying relationships: Lady Dedlock and her family solicitor, Mr. Tulkinghorn.
This is a battle conducted entirely in stillness — two people in the same room, saying almost nothing, and yet the danger between them is almost physical.
With me to unpack it are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the perspective of a lifetime of literary scholarship and a deep commitment to reading Dickens as a moralist above all.
Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more of Dickens than perhaps anyone alive, and hears in every page exactly how it wants to be performed.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a critic and close reader who has lived with this novel since her teens and never stopped finding new things in it.
Edmund, let's begin with Tulkinghorn — because Dickens introduces him here in a way that is quite extraordinary.
Thank you. And yes — Tulkinghorn's arrival at Chesney Wold in this passage is, I think, one of the finest entrances in all of English fiction.
Dickens gives him a pace that is, as he tells us precisely, never quickened, never slackened.
He wears his usual expressionless mask — if it be a mask.
That parenthetical — if it be a mask — is the most unsettling three words Dickens might have chosen.
Because the alternative is worse: that there is no mask — that Tulkinghorn simply is that blankness.
And then we get the sentence I find most remarkable — Dickens tells us,
He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress.
The secrets are not in his head, not in his files — they are in his very body. That is Gothic of the highest order.
Edmund has put his finger on something crucial about how that passage performs — and I mean performs quite literally.
When you read that sentence aloud — he carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress — the rhythm does something rather sinister.
It accumulates. Every limb. Every crease. The repetition is almost ritualistic.
And then Dickens gives us this extraordinary self-referential moment — he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
He keeps it, as he keeps the secrets of his clients; he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself.
He is his own client. It's almost a legal joke — except that with Tulkinghorn, no joke is quite safe.
What strikes me every time I come back to this passage is how much Dickens gives us without giving us anything at all.
We don't know what Tulkinghorn knows about Lady Dedlock at this point. We can't be certain he knows anything.
And yet Dickens has already made him feel omniscient — omniscient and malign.
Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret.
That sentence has always made me slightly cold.
Because Dickens won't tell us either. We are in the same position as Lady Dedlock — we simply cannot read him.
That point about the reader being placed in Lady Dedlock's position is exactly where I want to go next.
Because in the dialogue passage — chapter twelve — we get the two of them in the same room, after her near-exposure, and the tension is almost unbearable.
Oliver, you've read this scene many times for performance. What does it feel like from the inside?
It's one of those passages where the prose does everything and the characters are allowed to do almost nothing.
Sir Leicester sits there looking at the fire with — and this is perfect — the general expression of the Dedlock on the staircase.
He's a portrait of himself. He doesn't even register as a person in the room, only as an emblem.
And while he gazes into the fire, the real drama is happening across the room in absolute silence.
Dickens describes it with that extraordinary accumulation of parallel clauses — listen to what he does here,
Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another.
Without any other alteration. Their faces betray nothing — and yet they are the most watched people in the room. It's theatre of a very high order.
Oliver is right to praise the dramatic compression. But I'd add something about what Sir Leicester represents in that moment.
His stately protest — that no association in my Lady's mind can possibly be traceable to this poor wretch — is comic, yes.
But it is also rather pitiable. He is protecting a world that is already crumbling, and he has no idea.
The Dedlock on the staircase — that phrase — is Dickens at his most precise. The ancestral portraits are their own commentary on everything Leicester believes in.
And Lady Dedlock's secret, if it breaks, will not merely ruin her. It will unmake him — his dignity, his honour, his entire understanding of himself.
Edmund's point about Sir Leicester is important because it reminds us that Lady Dedlock is not only protecting herself.
And the passage that follows — where they meet again and again over subsequent days — shows how complete a performance this becomes.
Dickens describes her with that wonderful phrase — the exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers.
Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine.
There's something almost unbearably sad about that phrase — presiding at her own shrine. As if she's already dead. As if the performance has swallowed the person.
And across from her, Tulkinghorn: the speechless repository of noble confidences — so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.
The paradox of that phrase is everything: he is the only person in the room who truly belongs there, because he holds what everyone else only displays.
And then Dickens brings the two threads together in that long, looping sentence that ends the passage.
It's almost musical in its construction — a series of questions that pile up and then close down, unanswered.
I'll read it slowly — because it deserves that.

But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares;
what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts.
For the time. Those two words. Dickens tells you the ending is coming, without telling you when.
It's the most elegant act of narrative foreshadowing I've encountered in this novel. And this novel is full of them.
Oliver's right, and I don't want to argue with the performance instinct here, because it's exactly correct.
But I'd want to insist on something moral in that structure as well. Those repeated questions — what each would give to know — are not only suspense.
They are an anatomy of what secrets do to people. The concealment isn't protecting Lady Dedlock — it's consuming her.
And it is consuming Tulkinghorn too, though he would never admit to being consumed by anything.
Dickens is always, at heart, a novelist of character under pressure. This is what that pressure looks like from the outside — perfectly composed, absolutely treacherous.
Consuming is the right word, I think. And there's something important to say about what lies beneath the composure — the secret itself, the life Lady Dedlock has buried.
Caroline, Edmund, Oliver — before we move on, is there a final thought each of you would want to leave listeners with about this relationship?
For me it's the insolent grace — that phrase Dickens uses when she passes close to Tulkinghorn.
She passes close to him, with her usual fatigued manner and insolent grace.
In those five words — insolent grace — is her whole character and her whole tragedy. She will not flinch. She will not yield. And it will destroy her.
I'd stay with the image of Tulkinghorn walking at his unvarying pace.
Never quickened, never slackened. It is the image of a man who believes time is entirely on his side. And for the greater part of the novel, he is correct.
And I'd go back to that parenthetical. If it be a mask. Three words that open an abyss.
As a performer you have to make a choice about Tulkinghorn — is he cold because he's trained himself to be, or cold because there is simply nothing warm in him at all?
Dickens refuses to decide. And that refusal is, I think, the most frightening thing in these chapters.
Concealment, composure, and the slow steady approach of someone who never needs to hurry.
It's a masterclass in Gothic tension — and we've barely begun to trace where it leads.
After the break, we'll turn to a very different kind of concealment — the secret kept not from an enemy, but from oneself.

segments.title: Laughter and Darkness: Skimpole and the Minor Figures

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We've been tracking the great comic grotesques of the novel — but this segment turns to something more unsettling.
The moments where laughter shades into foreboding, where tenderness carries the weight of doom.
Specifically, we're in Chapter Thirteen — Mr. Jarndyce speaks to Richard and Ada about their future.
It is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the novel.
Edmund Leigh is with us — the Oxford don who reads Dickens as a moralist first and always.
Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps any living person.
And Caroline Woodcourt, whose ear for the verbal music of this novel is second to none.
Edmund, let's begin with you. What is Jarndyce actually doing in this scene?
What Jarndyce is doing is one of the finest acts of moral generosity in the whole of Dickens.
He is not lecturing. He is not imposing.
He is, with extraordinary delicacy, giving two young people permission — permission to feel, and permission to change.
Listen to how he opens his confidence to them — it is worth attending to closely.

"When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here — don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear! — being in a mind to go through life together."
Afar off. He repeats it. That repetition is doing enormous work.
He is saying: I imagined this, yes — but I held it at a distance. I did not presume.
That is the hallmark of a certain kind of English virtue — the virtue of restraint practised not from coldness but from profound respect.
Edmund is absolutely right about that restraint — but what strikes me, performing this passage, is how deeply comic the interruption is.
"Don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!" — right in the middle of a solemn declaration.
That's Dickens the performer, you see. He cannot resist the human detail that makes the scene live.
And then he moves — effortlessly — into what is, I think, a genuinely great piece of moral counsel.
Jarndyce says — and I always feel the breath of real experience in this —

"if you DO change — if you DO come to find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and woman than you were as boy and girl — don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
Nothing monstrous or uncommon. What a quietly magnificent reassurance.
He is giving them a map for failure — not because he expects them to fail, but because he loves them enough to prepare them.
What moves me most reading this passage is how Jarndyce refuses to be the voice of doom.
He says as much — he could warn them about the thousand things that might divert them. But he will not.
That restraint — Oliver's word, and it's exactly right — is a form of faith in them.
And then, when he does counsel Richard directly, the language becomes almost Biblical in its plainness.
He says — and I think this is where the scene becomes something more than tender —
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner. It's such a strange, particular image — and yet it lands perfectly.
Because we already know, as readers, that Richard will be precisely the man who separates the two.
Caroline touches on something I consider central to the moral architecture of this novel.
Jarndyce's counsel to Richard is not merely paternal warmth. It is a diagnosis.
Dickens sees — and gives Jarndyce the language to articulate — the precise moral deficiency that will undo Richard.
It is the inability to mean what one undertakes. To set about a thing with genuine commitment.
Jarndyce says it almost with the directness of a schoolmaster — and I mean that as the highest compliment.
"If you had the abilities of all the great men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely meaning it and setting about it."
That is Johnson's wisdom dressed in Dickens's prose. And it is every bit as good.
And then Dickens does something extraordinary — something that only he would risk at this moment.
After all that warmth and counsel, Esther watches Richard and Ada walk away — and Dickens turns the light off.
Quite literally turns the light off. Listen to this.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness.
So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
The room darkened as they went out. He just — does that.
No authorial commentary. No nudge to the reader. The world itself mourns what the reader already dreads.
That passage stops me every time. Every single time.
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone." — five words, and the whole novel turns.
What I love — what I find almost unbearable — is the word lightly. They went on lightly.
They have no idea. They are walking into the shadow with a lightness that is itself the tragedy.
And Esther watches. She always watches. That is her particular burden in this novel.
The device — and it is a masterly device — of filtering this through Esther's narration is what gives it its peculiar pathos.
Had Dickens employed his omniscient narrator here, the effect would be merely ironic. Clever, perhaps. But cold.
Because Esther loves them. She loves Richard. She loves Ada with something approaching maternal devotion.
So when she watches the room darken, we feel the darkness fall through her feeling. That is irreplaceable.
Edmund, Caroline, Oliver — what a passage to inhabit together.
The sunlight, the counsel, the shadow at the end — all of it pointing forward to what the novel will do to Richard Carstone.
Jarndyce offers the map. Richard will refuse to read it. And the room darkens accordingly.
We'll be back shortly to pursue where that shadow leads.

segments.title: Jo's Erasure: Class, Suffering, and the Law

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes one of the great English novels apart, slowly and with pleasure.
Today we're deep inside the novel's great preoccupation — what happens to those the law cannot see, and will not protect.
At the centre of this segment is Jo — the crossing-sweeper, the boy who knows nothing, and who is perhaps the novel's most devastating moral argument.
With me, as ever, are three distinguished readers of this novel.
Sir Edmund Leigh, the retired Oxford don who reads novels as explorations of moral character first and social thesis a distant second.
Oliver Trevelyan, actor and narrator, who has performed more of the canon aloud than almost anyone alive, and hears the music in every sentence.
And Caroline Woodcourt, critic and devoted re-reader, who is never afraid to say what moves her, and what the novel owes its characters.
We begin with the inquest into Nemo's death, and the moment Jo is turned away as a witness because he cannot say what will be done to him in a court of law.
Edmund, I thought we might start with you — because what happens to Jo at this inquest is, I think, both a legal fact and a moral indictment.
Yes, and the narrator's response to that indictment is remarkable in its restraint.
The novelist does not rage at the magistrate or harangue the reader.
He turns, quietly, to the boy himself, and addresses him directly.
The passage reads, in its entirety:
"Jo, is it thou? Well, well! Though a rejected witness, who can't exactly say what will be done to him in greater hands than men's, thou art not quite in outer darkness."
There is a Biblical register there — "outer darkness" — that places Jo, the illiterate crossing-sweeper, into a theological frame.
The law has dismissed him. But grace, the narrator implies, has not.
And that distinction matters enormously — not as social polemic, but as moral vision.
What strikes me — and I've read this passage many times — is the way the narrator earns the right to address Jo directly.
Because immediately before, we've had the testimony of Mrs. Piper.
And Mrs. Piper is — I mean, she is a masterpiece of comic vindictiveness.
She testifies, in her wonderful unpunctuated way, that the dead man — whom she insists on calling "the plaintive" —
"was reported to have sold himself."
She has dreamed of him taking a pick-axe from his pocket to split Johnny's head, and yet she has never actually seen him harm a soul.
The comedy is in the gap between her fertile terror and the reality she admits.
And after all that noise, all that self-serving parenthetical rambling, the narrator turns to Jo with — almost — tenderness.
Mrs. Piper is one of the great comic witness testimonies in English literature, and I say that having performed a good many of them.
"Chiefly in parentheses and without punctuation" — the narrator has already laughed at her before she opens her mouth.
But when you come to read the passages about Jo and the dead man, the performance demand shifts entirely.
Listen to what the boy knows of the man who died.
"That one cold winter night when he, the boy, was shivering in a doorway near his crossing, the man turned to look at him, and came back."
"Came back" — two words. That is the whole story of Nemo's goodness.
And then the man spoke — finding that the boy had not a friend in the world —
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging.
I have read that line in studio more than once, and I have had to stop.
That is precisely where the sentimentalist charge against this novelist collapses, I think.
One can accuse a writer of manipulating emotion. One cannot level that charge at four words.
"Neither have I. Not one." The symmetry between the outcast man and the outcast boy is established without a syllable of commentary.
And the narrator, when he returns to address Jo at the close of that chapter, uses the language not of outrage but of something rather older.
He speaks of "a distant ray of light" in the boy's loyalty to the dead man.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
That is not a political pamphlet. That is charity, in the theological sense.
I agree — and I want to sit with the dialect for a moment.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos." The misspelling is not mockery.
It is the novelist insisting that we hear Jo's voice exactly as it was — unschooled, unpolished, and entirely true.
The law rejected Jo because he could not articulate the oath.
But what Jo says about the dead man is the most articulate thing in the entire chapter.
That is the novelist's trick — and it is a trick, a very great one — of encoding the moral argument in the testimony that was legally excluded.
Jo can't say what will be done to him in a court of law.
But the reader knows precisely what the novelist thinks should be done to a society that cannot protect a boy who grieves like that.
Now, what strikes me is that this erasure of the vulnerable by institutional process isn't confined to Jo.
The moment when Mrs. Rouncewell pleads with Lady Dedlock for her son's life is another version of the same helplessness before power.
Yes — and Mrs. Rouncewell's plea is, for my money, one of the finest passages of humble eloquence in the novel.
She knows her station. She knows Lady Dedlock's remoteness.
And yet she says to her mistress, with perfect dignity:

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
The housekeeper understands the class architecture she inhabits precisely.
She appeals not against that architecture, but through it — invoking service and love as the only currency she has.
And yet what the scene quietly indicts is the system that makes such a plea necessary at all.
A mother is on her knees — figuratively, at least — before someone who may hold the key to her son's freedom.
And the information that might save him is caught in the same web of pride and propriety that the whole novel traces.
That phrase — "you go your own way always without help" — is heartbreaking as much as it is accurate.
Lady Dedlock is not cruel. She is simply constitutionally alone.
Which brings us — and I think it always comes back to this — to the question of what the novel thinks law is actually for.
Jarndyce puts it with extraordinary brevity.
"The plain truth is, I have forsworn and abjured the whole business these many years, and my soul is sick of it."
"My soul is sick of it." Not my patience. Not my purse. His soul.
That is a man who understands that prolonged contact with this system is a moral contamination.
And yet he does the right thing immediately — he submits the will at once, without drama, without ceremony.
Jarndyce is, for me, the novel's moral centre — and precisely because he is not a hero in any conventional sense.
He does not fight the system. He refuses to be consumed by it.
That distinction — refusal rather than rebellion — is what Burke might have called the wisdom of the experienced temperament.
He does not abolish Chancery. He simply will not let it touch his soul.
That image of the soul as the last inviolable territory — exempt from the court's jurisdiction — is a wonderful place to pause.
We've moved from Jo — rejected by the law as a witness — to Mrs. Rouncewell, pleading across the barriers of class, to Jarndyce's quiet moral refusal.
In the next segment, we turn to how the novel renders suffering on the page — the prose style itself as an act of moral attention.

segments.title: Dickens's Architecture: Chance, Connection, and Design

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel apart — carefully — to see what makes it tick.
Today we're looking at something that sits right at the heart of Dickens's achievement in this novel: the question of design.
How does he build a world so enormous, so teeming — and make it feel, against all odds, inevitable?
With me today are three readers who know this novel very well indeed.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and literary critic of the old school — a man who believes the novel's first obligation is to its characters, not its causes.
Oliver Trevelyan has voiced more classic novels than perhaps any living actor — he comes to Dickens as a performer, hearing the rhythms that most readers only sense.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has returned to Bleak House many times over many years — she brings the attentiveness of a reader who loves the prose as prose.
Let's begin where the novel begins — with that extraordinary opening.
I've read that opening more times than I can count, and it still stops me cold every single time.
Dickens doesn't begin with a character, doesn't begin with a plot — he begins with a condition.
London. Implacable November weather. Just those fragments — hammered in like nails.
And then — the thing that makes performers weep with envy — he does this:
A forty-foot prehistoric lizard waddling up Holborn Hill.
It's absurd — and yet it isn't absurd at all, because the fog and the mud have already made that world feel prehistoric.
The joke earns its keep because the atmosphere has prepared it perfectly.
That's well observed, and I want to press on that word 'absurd,' because I think it obscures something more interesting.
The Megalosaurus is not a joke, precisely — it is a moral proposition delivered in comic dress.
Dickens is telling us that this world has reverted — that civilisation here is merely a crust over something much older and more savage.
Notice too what he does with the mud — it accumulates, in his own phrase, at compound interest.
"accumulating at compound interest."
He borrows the language of finance to describe physical corruption — and that borrowing is entirely deliberate.
The novel's great subject — the way institutions decay and proliferate like organic matter — is present from the very first paragraph.
What strikes me most, returning to it again, is the sentence — or rather the non-sentence — quality of that opening.
Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better. Foot passengers, jostling.
No verbs to carry things forward — everything is simply there, present, inert.
It's as if grammar itself has broken down under the weight of all this mud and fog.
And then there's this astonishing image — the sun in mourning.
"making a soft black drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown snowflakes — gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of the sun."
The death of the sun. In the first page. Dickens is not being subtle about what kind of novel this is going to be.
That architecture of doom established in the opening — Dickens then populates it with characters who seem to exist in a completely different register.
Lawrence Boythorn is about as far from gothic atmosphere as it's possible to get — and yet he belongs to the same novel.
Oliver, Boythorn is a character made for a performer.
He is — he is absolutely made for a performer, and I say that as someone who has played him more than once.
The secret of Boythorn is that he has no irony about himself whatsoever — and Dickens has total irony about him.
That gap is where all the comedy lives.
His account of the dispute with Sir Leicester — every escalation delivered with absolute conviction — is a masterpiece of comic timing on the page.
Listen to how it builds:
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
The parallel structure — his action, my action, his action, my action — it's practically musical.
And then that laugh — written into the prose — Ha, ha, ha! — Dickens insisting you hear it aloud.
Boythorn is — I must be honest — one of the few characters in this novel I find purely delightful without reservation.
But I would push back slightly on the idea that the comedy is merely entertainment.
The dispute with Sir Leicester is, at its core, a dispute about property, privilege, and the law's complicity in both.
Boythorn's magnificent absurdity — the fire engine, the man traps, the chopping and burning of gates — is his refusal to be governed by a system that serves the baronet above the honest man.
Dickens makes it funny so that we enjoy the rebellion before we understand it.
What I love is that line about Sir Leicester and his forebears — the insults are so elaborately stacked.
Dickens gives Boythorn this extraordinary battery of abuse — and then has him compare Sir Leicester to ivory balls in a Chinese carving, nested one inside another.
"he should not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory balls in a Chinese carving."
The image is both perfectly specific and wonderfully ridiculous — which is Boythorn exactly.
He contains multitudes — all of them equally indignant.
The comedy of Boythorn sits alongside something much darker — the novel's deep preoccupation with secrets and the damage they do.
Lady Dedlock's story threads through the whole novel — and it begins, almost imperceptibly, with a very small revelation.
Caroline, you've written about the way Dickens manages suspense — how does the Tulkinghorn scene work?
It's one of the great demonstrations of what Dickens can do with almost nothing.
Sir Leicester is reading a letter from Tulkinghorn — fumbling with his eyeglass, losing his place — and then he arrives at the sentence that changes everything.
The reader has already seen Lady Dedlock's face when she glimpsed that handwriting — we know what this means even if Sir Leicester does not.
And then Tulkinghorn's words land — read aloud by an oblivious husband to the woman they are designed to unmask:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
I have seen him. Three words. That's all it takes.
And the reader feels Lady Dedlock's terror before she has to show it on the page.
The theatrical term is dramatic irony, and Dickens handles it here with the confidence of someone who had actually performed this material before audiences.
What's genius is the comedy of Sir Leicester fumbling — losing the page, dropping the thread — because it delays the blow just long enough to be unbearable.
The reader is ahead of him. Lady Dedlock is ahead of him. And he's adjusting his eyeglass.
It's almost cruel — which is exactly what great suspense requires.
I want to connect this to the passage from Chapter Seventeen — about the disclosure made to Jarndyce concerning Esther's origins.
Dickens is building what one might call an architecture of concealment — and the stone that holds the arch together is a woman's determination never to speak.
Jarndyce reports what he was told by the lady — who will not even give her real name — with a kind of awed simplicity:

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
The steadfastness of her resolution. Dickens gives Lady Dedlock a kind of terrible integrity — her secret is her self-punishment as much as her self-protection.
This is what I mean when I say Dickens's deepest subject is always character — what a person chooses to carry, and what the carrying costs.
Yes — and I think what Dickens understands is that the silence is not passive. It is an act of will, repeated every day.
Lady Dedlock has constructed her entire self around an absence — and the novel slowly undoes that construction.
By the time we reach the late chapters — George moving through the empty rooms at Chesney Wold — the cost of all that concealment is written on the very walls of the house.
That late passage — George carrying his light through the darkened house — is, I think, among the finest things in the novel.
It gathers everything: the dead Tulkinghorn, the vanished Lady Dedlock, the stricken Sir Leicester — all of it present in the absence.
And Dickens finds exactly the right image for what George feels as he moves through these charged empty rooms:
"he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
Blank as the darkness above and below. The house has become a kind of void — not haunted, which would be a comfort, but simply emptied.
The gothic atmosphere of the opening has, by the novel's end, migrated inside — it is now the atmosphere of consequence.
What gets me, reading that aloud, is the rhythm of the repetition — blank, blank — it's almost incantatory.
And George is the perfect witness for this moment — a soldier, a man of physical action, now reduced to moving slowly through rooms with a lamp.
He's looking for something that might be there — and isn't. The novel has its own foreboding: 'Who will tell him?'
Dickens writes that question into George's mind — and leaves it hanging over the whole scene.
That is what great novelists do — they make the silence speak louder than anything that could be said.
Fog at the opening, blankness at the end — the same atmosphere, deepened into something tragic by everything the novel has done in between.
That's the architecture: Dickens builds a world so completely that its weather becomes its moral weather.
Thank you all — we'll continue shortly, looking more closely at the characters who move through that world and what they reveal about each other.
We've spent this episode tracing the web of connections that Dickens draws across Bleak House — connections that bind characters to each other, and to consequences they cannot foresee.
I want to close with something that I think sits at the very heart of this novel: the weight of consequence.
The way that small acts — a handkerchief laid over a sleeping child, a promise made in tenderness, a young man's easy temperament — ripple outward into lives transformed.
Edmund, I'd like to begin with you — and with Esther, and a moment that Dickens charges with a kind of terrible retrospective irony.
Thank you. There is a passage in Esther's narrative that I find almost unbearably affecting — and I use that word advisedly, because Dickens earns it absolutely.
Esther stands in a brickmaker's cottage, looking at a dead infant — a child she and Ada have tried to comfort — and she performs a tiny act of tenderness.
She lays her handkerchief over the child. That is all. A small, human gesture.
But Esther, narrating from the future, tells us — with devastating quietness — what she did not yet know.
"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head—"
"—how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
That phrase — "unquiet bosom" against "motionless and peaceful breast" — is Dickens at his most morally precise.
The handkerchief passes from a dead child to a living fugitive. The object carries the weight of both.
That passage stopped me cold the first time I read it. And every subsequent time, I confess, it stops me again.
What Dickens is doing with Esther's narrative voice is extraordinarily subtle. She is a narrator who knows the end of her own story.
And she deploys that foreknowledge with tremendous restraint — she never tells us what she knows, only that she did not know it then.
The halo she sees around the child, through Ada's hair — that image is so tender it almost breaks your heart before the irony lands.
And then there is that ending — Esther and Ada leaving, and the woman at the door, murmuring her old soothing words: "Jenny, Jenny!"
The repetition of a name. The simplest thing. And somehow the most heartbreaking in the whole passage.
Caroline is right to identify the restraint. It is, if I may say so, the opposite of sentimentality — though the scene is drenched in feeling.
Dickens trusts the object — the handkerchief — to carry the moral meaning across the entire novel. That is structural genius.
And note: it is also an act of individual virtue that Dickens honours. Esther's pity, Ada's pity — these are not abstractions. They are persons choosing goodness.
I want to pick up this thread of consequence and pull it in a different direction — toward Richard Carstone, and a scene that breaks my heart for entirely different reasons.
Early in the novel, Esther sits between Richard and Ada while they are young, and besotted, and full of ardent promises.
The comedy of it is real — they have essentially fallen in love with Esther as well as with each other, they're so confiding.
But listen to what Esther tells us they talked of, because Dickens buries the future in the language of the present.
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself —"
"— and then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could come to anything —"

"— and how it could come to happiness only if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Constancy. Fortitude. Perseverance. Three words that, knowing what becomes of Richard, land like three small stones on a grave.
That's exactly it. Richard will work his fingers to the bone, he says. Ada says it too. And you want to believe them.
The scene is so warm. Dickens makes you feel the warmth of it — the three of them up half the night, advising and talking.
That word "wild" — "their own wild way" — is doing a great deal of work. It's affectionate, but it contains a warning Esther cannot yet name.
Richard's ruin is never sudden. It's a slow drift — a reluctance to apply the very constancy and perseverance that this lovely night asks of him.
And the novel gives us the diagnosis in advance — remarkably early, and from a rather unexpected source.
Mrs. Bayham Badger — wonderful woman, not a word wasted — delivers it with the efficiency of a clinical report.
She tells Esther that Richard does not have that positive interest in medicine that makes it his vocation — that he finds it, in essence, tiresome.
And then she offers the contrast — and it's pointed, almost merciless — in the figure of a certain young surgeon.
"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money —"
"— and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Endurance and disappointment. And we know, by the time we reach this passage, that Woodcourt will endure. Richard will not.
Mrs. Badger's speech is a small masterpiece of what I would call moral characterisation by proxy — she defines Richard by contrast with a better man, and she does so without malice.
Richard is not wicked. That is precisely what makes his fate so melancholy. He is simply easy — too easy, too yielding — and the Chancery suit is perfectly designed to exploit that ease.
Dickens understood that the great destroyer of character is not villainy but drift — the long, unresisted pull of irresolution.
And Woodcourt stands beside him in the novel — not as a reproach, exactly, but as a kind of quiet alternative: what earnest purpose looks like when it is sustained.
What strikes me, listening to all three of you, is how insistently this novel refuses to let the smallest moment pass without consequence.
A handkerchief. A night of young promises. A doctor's easy temperament. Each of these things travels through the novel and returns, changed.
Bleak House asks us to attend — to the texture of moments, to the words characters choose, to the objects they hold.
Because in Dickens's world, nothing is accidental and nothing is lost — everything accumulates, and everything, eventually, must be reckoned with.
My thanks to Edmund Leigh, Oliver Trevelyan, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has been, throughout, a genuine pleasure.
And to you, our listeners — thank you for spending time with us inside the fog and the fog-horn world of Bleak House.

The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.
c6:p46.summary: Detailed description of Bleak House's furnishings in each room, establishing a warm, hospitable environment filled with quirky collections and careful comfort.

c7:p59.text:
“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”
c7:p59.summary: The crippled lady, after her husband finds her on the pavement, looks at him coldly and curses the Dedlock family: she will walk the terrace forever as a warning of coming calamity and disgrace.
c7:p59.best_quote: I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!

Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don’t know that everybody
has two names. Never heerd of sich a think. Don’t know that Jo is

“Then make it easy for her!” growled the man upon the floor. “I wants
it done, and over. I wants a end of these liberties took with my
place. I wants an end of being drawed like a badger. Now you’re
a-going to poll-pry and question according to custom—I know what
you’re a-going to be up to. Well! You haven’t got no occasion to be
up to it. I’ll save you the trouble. Is my daughter a-washin? Yes,
she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That’s wot we drinks.
How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead! An’t my
place dirty? Yes, it is dirty—it’s nat’rally dirty, and it’s
nat’rally onwholesome; and we’ve had five dirty and onwholesome
children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them,
and for us besides. Have I read the little book wot you left? No, I
an’t read the little book wot you left. There an’t nobody here as
knows how to read it; and if there wos, it wouldn’t be suitable to
me. It’s a book fit for a babby, and I’m not a babby. If you was to
leave me a doll, I shouldn’t nuss it. How have I been conducting of
myself? Why, I’ve been drunk for three days; and I’da been drunk four
if I’da had the money. Don’t I never mean for to go to church? No, I
don’t never mean for to go to church. I shouldn’t be expected there,
if I did; the beadle’s too gen-teel for me. And how did my wife get
that black eye? Why, I give it her; and if she says I didn’t, she’s a
Lie!”

During this dialogue Mr. Tulkinghorn has stood aloof by the old
portmanteau, with his hands behind him, equally removed, to all
appearance, from all three kinds of interest exhibited near the
bed—from the young surgeon’s professional interest in death,
noticeable as being quite apart from his remarks on the deceased as
an individual; from the old man’s unction; and the little crazy
woman’s awe. His imperturbable face has been as inexpressive as his
rusty clothes. One could not even say he has been thinking all this

the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case,

“Pardon me,” returned Mr. Vholes, going on in exactly the same inward
and dispassionate manner. “Mr. C. takes certain interests under
certain wills disputed in the suit. It is a term we use. In reference
to Mr. C,’s pursuit of his interests, I mentioned to you, Miss
Summerson, the first time I had the pleasure of seeing you, in my
desire that everything should be openly carried on—I used those
words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to
thank you very much, sir!”
c60:p94.summary: Vholes meticulously documents his conversation in his diary and explains that he must openly declare his belief that Richard's affairs are in very bad way and the marriage was ill-advised, all as professional duty; he then abruptly switches to greeting Richard's arrival.

c58:p70.text:
His formal array of words might have at any other time, as it has
often had, something ludicrous in it, but at this time it is serious
and affecting. His noble earnestness, his fidelity, his gallant
shielding of her, his generous conquest of his own wrong and his own
pride for her sake, are simply honourable, manly, and true. Nothing
less worthy can be seen through the lustre of such qualities in the
commonest mechanic, nothing less worthy can be seen in the best-born
gentleman. In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both
children of the dust shine equally.
c58:p70.summary: The narrator reflects that Sir Leicester's earnestness, fidelity, and generous conquering of his own pride for Lady Dedlock's sake transcend class and honor all humanity.
c58:p70.best_quote: "In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."

c56:p51.text:
“Now, Mr. Jarndyce”—Mr. Bucket has read his face with the greatest
attention all along—“I speak to you as a gentleman of a humane
heart, and under such pressing circumstances as don’t often happen.
If ever delay was dangerous, it’s dangerous now; and if ever you
couldn’t afterwards forgive yourself for causing it, this is the
time. Eight or ten hours, worth, as I tell you, a hundred pound
apiece at least, have been lost since Lady Dedlock disappeared. I am
charged to find her. I am Inspector Bucket. Besides all the rest
that’s heavy on her, she has upon her, as she believes, suspicion of
murder. If I follow her alone, she, being in ignorance of what Sir
Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, has communicated to me, may be driven to
desperation. But if I follow her in company with a young lady,
answering to the description of a young lady that she has a
tenderness for—I ask no question, and I say no more than that—she
will give me credit for being friendly. Let me come up with her and
be able to have the hold upon her of putting that young lady for’ard,
and I’ll save her and prevail with her if she is alive. Let me come
up with her alone—a hard matter—and I’ll do my best, but I don’t
answer for what the best may be. Time flies; it’s getting on for one
o’clock. When one strikes, there’s another hour gone, and it’s worth
a thousand pound now instead of a hundred.”

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I
will assume that a few years hence you will be in your hearts to one
another what you are to-day. All I say before speaking to you
according to that assumption is, if you DO change—if you DO come to
find that you are more commonplace cousins to each other as man and
woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be
nothing monstrous or uncommon in it. I am only your friend and
distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever. But I wish and
hope to retain your confidence if I do nothing to forfeit it.”

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.

“By my soul,” exclaimed Mr. Boythorn, suddenly firing another volley,
“that fellow is, and his father was, and his grandfather was, the
most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by
some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but
a walking-stick’s! The whole of that family are the most solemnly
conceited and consummate blockheads! But it’s no matter; he should
not shut up my path if he were fifty baronets melted into one and
living in a hundred Chesney Wolds, one within another, like the ivory
balls in a Chinese carving. The fellow, by his agent, or secretary,
or somebody, writes to me ‘Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, presents
his compliments to Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, and has to call his
attention to the fact that the green pathway by the old
parsonage-house, now the property of Mr. Lawrence Boythorn, is Sir
Leicester’s right of way, being in fact a portion of the park of
Chesney Wold, and that Sir Leicester finds it convenient to close up
the same.’ I write to the fellow, ‘Mr. Lawrence Boythorn presents his
compliments to Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, and has to call HIS
attention to the fact that he totally denies the whole of Sir
Leicester Dedlock’s positions on every possible subject and has to
add, in reference to closing up the pathway, that he will be glad to
see the man who may undertake to do it.’ The fellow sends a most
abandoned villain with one eye to construct a gateway. I play upon
that execrable scoundrel with a fire-engine until the breath is
nearly driven out of his body. The fellow erects a gate in the night.
I chop it down and burn it in the morning. He sends his myrmidons to
come over the fence and pass and repass. I catch them in humane man
traps, fire split peas at their legs, play upon them with the
engine—resolve to free mankind from the insupportable burden of the
existence of those lurking ruffians. He brings actions for trespass;
I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and
battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha,
ha!”

The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
